column3: Resto shamans were considered an
extremely valuable healer in vanilla.
However, much of their appeal came from
their raid utility spells rather than
their healing output. But, things are
different in Burning Crusade and resto
shamans have become a different beast
entirely. And I'm sure you've heard that
already, but what else? What else makes
shaman a compelling choice compared to
the other three healers? That's what
we'll explore in this video. We'll start
off by looking at the spells that you'll
be regularly using as a resto shaman.
The first is chain heal. This iconic
ability heals your initial target for a
fairly large amount and then attempts to
jump to two nearby injured targets. Each
time chain heal jumps, the effectiveness
of the heal is reduced by 50%. There are
three requirements for chain heal to
jump after it heals its initial target.
There has to be at least one player
who's a part of the initial chain heal
target's group below 100% HP and within
15 yards of the initial chain heal
target. But, what if there are multiple
group members within 15 yards of the
initial target and below 100% HP? Who
does it go to? Well, chain heal is a
smart heal, so it will always jump to
the target with the lowest HP when given
the choice. After that first jump, chain
heal can jump a second time to heal a
third target. The heal on the first jump
target is reduced by 50% and the heal on
the second jump target is reduced by
25%. I know that's a little confusing,
so I put together an example. Suppose
that player A, player B, and player C
belong to the same group and are all
within 15 yards of each other. Player A
is missing 1,500 HP, player B is missing
1,000, and player C is missing 750. For
the sake of this example, assume that
your chain heal heals for an average of
2,000. In this scenario, you should cast
chain heal on player A since they're
missing the most HP and the initial hit
is always 100% effective. If you've been
following along so far, you'll know that
chain heal will then jump from player A
to player B. Since player B is missing
more hit points than player C, chain
heal heals player B for 1,000 and then
jumps to player C. Player C is then
healed for 500 and the chain ends there.
It's important to note here that the
initial heal and the subsequent jumps
are all occurring simultaneously. I know
that I'm making it seem like there's a
delay between the heals, but that's just
so you can visualize what's going on
behind the scenes. There are a couple of
smaller things that I wanted to mention
before moving on. If there are no
targets to jump to after the initial
heal and the Shaman that casted it is
below 100% HP, chain heal can actually
jump back to the Shaman regardless of
their proximity to the last link in the
chain. Also, all heals in the chain have
an independent chance to critically
strike. So, if your chain heal hits
three targets, there's a good chance
that at least one of those hits will be
a critical strike. And that's great for
Shaman since they have a talent that
causes their critical heals to leave a
powerful armor buff on their target.
We'll go into more detail about the
technical stuff associated with chain
heal in the last section. But first,
despite what you may have heard, Shamans
do in fact have other healing spells.
Healing Wave is their big single target
heal with a 2.5 second cast time thanks
to improved healing wave. The throughput
of this spell is greatly increased when
you take advantage of healing way. This
talent causes your successful healing
waves to apply a buff to the target that
increases the effect of subsequent
healing waves by 6%. This effect can
stack up to three times for a total of
18% increased effectiveness with healing
wave. This makes healing wave a much
more mana efficient spell when focusing
a single target. Healing Wave can also
function as an incredibly powerful
emergency heal when paired with Nature's
Swiftness. Nature's Swiftness is a
3-minute cooldown spell that makes your
next nature cast an instant cast. It has
no global cooldown, so you can macro
these two abilities together to
instantly top your target from critical
condition, all with the press of a
single button. By the way, if you want
to see a holy paladin guide, I already
have that done. You just have to
subscribe. I I don't know how many subs
I need for it to be released, but you
have to subscribe first because
that's what's that's what's going to
have to happen. Moving on, we have
lesser healing wave. This is the
shaman's fast but inefficient casted
heal. It starts off okay in the
beginning of the expansion, but quickly
declines as you get gear. That's because
it has a relatively low healing
coefficient compared to your other
spells, which means it won't scale as
well with bonus healing. That doesn't
mean you shouldn't use this spell.
Sometimes it's worth sacrificing
throughput and efficiency for speed. For
example, if your target only has 2,000
HP and they're about to be targeted by a
mechanic that hits for 3,000, it's much
safer to heal that target with lesser
healing wave and then use an efficient
heal after. You should also consider
using this spell when the fight has
either a random movement mechanic or an
interrupt or a silence mechanic. Next up
is Earth Shield. This is a new shield
ability for the resto shaman in TBC, and
unlike other shaman shields, it can be
placed on another raid member. Earth
Shield has six charges and provides the
following benefits while it's active.
First, the target has a 30% increased
chance to ignore spell pushback. For
those of you who don't know, spell
pushback is the delay in spell casting
that occurs when you receive an attack,
and many casters have talents that
passively reduce it, but there are a few
who don't, and their DPS suffers
immensely on fights that cause a lot of
spell pushback. The most common specs
that fall under this category are
balance druids, elemental shamans,
shadow priests, UA warlocks, and frost
mages. So, Earth Shield is situationally
very useful for them, but there's more
to Earth Shield than passive spell
pushback reduction. The second benefit
is attacks made against the Earth Shield
target will consume a charge of the
shield, healing the target for a large
amount. A very important concept to
understand here is that when a charge of
Earth Shield is consumed, the heal on
the Earth Shielded target is attributed
to them and not the Shaman who cast it
Earth Shield. The reason why that's
important is because the Earth Shielded
target also assumes all threat
associated with that healing. That makes
this buff exceptional for putting on
tanks. It provides them with both
periodic healing and a ton of extra
threat throughout the fight. One minor
thing I wanted to mention about Earth
Shield is that it can be snapshotted.
That means that all six charges are
calculated using the bonus healing the
Shaman had when they originally casted
the shield and not when the charges are
actually consumed. That means you can
pop a couple of bonus healing trinkets,
drop Wrath of Air Totem, and cast Earth
Shield on the tank, then swap to your
regular gear all before the boss is
actually pulled. And yeah, it is pretty
sweaty, but the shield does last for a
minimum of 20 to 30 seconds on a tank.
And it's the little things like this
that keep healing interesting. Now, this
is a restoration guide, but I will
mention some Shaman utility spells that
you'll be making regular use of. The
first one is Water Shield. This is also
a new shield ability for TBC and it has
three charges. While it's active, the
shield provides a slightly ridiculous 50
MP5 and that's only part of what it
does. The other part is a charge-based
mechanic like Earth Shield, but it
returns mana instead of health. So,
whenever is hit by a ranged or melee
attack, a charge of the shield is
expended and the Shaman gains 204 mana.
An important thing to note here is that
Water Shield costs no mana. That means
you can refresh Water Shield when you're
outside of or trying to get outside of
the five-second rule. The second
non-healing spell that you'll be making
regular use of is Earth Shock. Earth
Shock has two components, a damage
component and a spell interruption
component. Only the damage component of
Earth Shock scales with the spell's
rank, and the spell interruption portion
remains the same from rank one to max
rank. This gives resto shamans access to
the shortest cooldown range interrupt in
the game for only 30 mana. You can
expect to be using this spell regularly
throughout your rating adventures, but
I'll leave you with an example of one
you'll encounter early on, the Moroes
encounter from Karazhan. This boss
starts with four adds. Each add has
their own set of abilities that must be
managed by the raid throughout the
fight. Your duty as a resto shaman is to
coordinate with other interrupters in
the raid to ensure that the following
casts never go off. That's mana burn
from this chick, greater heal from this
chick, and holy light from this chick.
Tremor Totem is another invaluable asset
that the restoration shaman brings to a
raid group. While the totem is active,
it periodically removes all fear, charm,
and sleep effects on all party members
within 30 yards. This ability is a
game-changer on encounters like
Nightbane. His bellowing roar ability
fears all players within 35 yards for 4
seconds. Being feared in this fight is
particularly bad because there are
several mechanics that punish you for
standing in certain locations. For
example, there are various lava
cross-sections around the boss called
charred earth that deal heavy damage
over time to players standing in them.
There's also a frontal physical cleave
and breath of fire, so Tremor Totem
saves lives here. I saved my favorite
spell for last, Grounding Totem. When
the shaman drops this totem, the next
single target spell casted on any of the
shaman's nearby party members will be
redirected to the totem, destroying the
totem and negating the spell. The
spell's function, combined with its
absurdly low cooldown of 15 seconds,
makes it borderline broken on some
encounters. And there are certain fights
that I'd argue would be nearly
impossible without Grounding Totem. One
example is Lady Vashj. In phases one and
three of this encounter, Vashj will
randomly cast Shock Blast on your main
tank. Shock Blast deals approximately
9,500 damage and stuns the target for 5
seconds. Grounding Totem is the perfect
counter to this ability. All the Shaman
needs to do is make sure that they
immediately drop a new Grounding Totem
after the previous one is destroyed from
absorbing Shock Blast. So, with
Grounding Totem, we can completely
bypass certain raid mechanics. Pretty
strong if you ask me. This is the last
section, healing assignments. Shamans
are incredible raid healers, but that's
not the only assignment that you'll get,
at least early on. Tank and single
target spot healing is a very common
assignment in Karazhan since there
aren't many mechanics that take
advantage of Chain Heal. Luckily, the
resto Shaman has excellent tools for
tank healing and the rotation is easy to
execute. Your first priority is to keep
up Earth Shield on your assigned target
at all times. This is usually one of the
tanks, but as we discussed before, there
are other viable targets in certain
situations. Whenever physical damage is
present, you should always maintain
Ancestral Fortitude on your assigned
tank. You should also aim to maintain
three stacks of Healing Wave on your
assigned tank at all times. A tip here
is you can use rank one Healing Wave to
fish for Ancestral Fortitude procs, as
well as maintain Healing Wave stacks for
a very low mana cost. As for healing
spells, you'll primarily be using
Healing Wave. Sometimes you'll use
Lesser Healing Wave or Chain Heal when
the situation calls for it, but Healing
Wave is often the go-to heal. To really
master the tank healing role, though,
you need to know how to downrank your
heals. You see, damage comes in all
shapes and sizes, and if you only use
your max rank spells, you'll end up with
a ton of overhealing and wasted mana.
That's why we downrank. For Healing
Wave, we typically use a mixture of rank
seven and rank eight to deal with
moderate to slightly higher amounts of
damage, but that's only if your target
has three stacks of Healing Wave. If
your target has no stacks of Healing
Wave, the mana efficiency of Healing
Wave rank seven and eight is only
slightly better than lesser healing wave
rank six and seven. So, you'll have to
use your discretion there. You'll use
your max rank healing wave when you need
to heal huge amounts of sustained
damage, which happens quite frequently
as a tank healer. This assignment is
typically short-lived and you should
only expect to get it in phase one.
After that, you're pretty much only raid
healing for the rest of the expansion,
but that doesn't mean you won't be
healing tanks anymore. Far from it,
actually. Remember that chain heal is a
smart heal and since tank are almost
always 100% HP, you'll be healing them
frequently, whether you like it or not.
They're often the best target to cast
chain heal on since the initial heal is
less likely to overheal them compared to
other targets. And they're usually
grouped up with melee and melee tend to
take a lot of splash damage. Now that
we've transitioned to raid healing and
spamming chain heal, we need to learn
how to down rank chain heal. The most
commonly used down rank is chain heal
rank four. That's because rank four
narrowly escapes the threshold for the
down rank penalty, which means that it
still benefits from all of your bonus
healing gear and it costs 20% less mana
than chain heal rank five. Chain heal
rank five does have slightly higher HPS
than rank four, so consider using it
when raw throughput takes priority over
efficiency. And just like with healing
wave, you can macro nature's swiftness
to chain heal rank five for a huge
emergency AoE burst heal. Down ranking
beyond rank four is viable, but due to
the down ranking penalty on those lower
ranks, it really depends on what gear
you have and as a result, I can't make a
solid recommendation. I did make a
detailed spreadsheet with the math and
rationale I use for my down ranking, so
